Q: Bulk email campaign manager architecture in Symfony: SMTP vs dedicated email providers A:

One more thought: suppose you build it yourself, and experience a serious bug that causes days of downtime while it's being fixed. That means your service doesn't operate for that time. This could be a big problem for your business.

Now suppose you engaged a service. They aren't immune from such outages either. So you could reduce your risk by engaging multiple services, and balancing your email campaigns over whichever ones are available. It's unlikely that all of them would be down at the same time, so you could in theory keep operating.

We did this with telephony at SchoolMessenger. We made automated phone calls and sent texts as well as using email. We had contracts with several bulk telephony companies, and our system was configurable quickly, so we could rebalance any time we needed to. We also had negotiated discounts with each vendor, in exchange for a certain minimum usage. So our system would track how much it used each service, and prefer the services we still needed to use to meet our minimum that quarter. After that, the service would route calls to the least expensive vendor for a given call.

Working with vendors creates a lot of new opportunities for optimization, but it isn't simple.

Q: Print function working on desktop but not mobile A:

I had the same problem. I think

window.print();

is blocking on desktop, but not on mobile devices. Also I think it's done for better performance on mobile devices.

Just use @media print block in CSS instead. Add some classes for changing elements and process it in this block

Q: language parameter is not working properly A:

The language=en parameter is only a language preference, not a strict guarantee. Google Geocoding may still return local-language names when English data is unavailable or when the local representation is considered more appropriate for that location. This is expected behavior for reverse geocoding. Reference Link

To improve consistency, you can:

  • Keep passing language=en.
  • Add region=in if the coordinates are in India and need India-specific results.
  • Use address_components and pick specific components like locality, administrative_area_level_1, country, etc, instead of relying only on formatted_address.
  • If strict English output is required, post-process or translate non-English components on your side.

Q: PyQt5 Table selected items doesn't include all selected items A:

Similarly to related "item" getter functions in QTableWidget (such as currentItem() or item()), QTableWidget only returns QTableWidgetItems that have been explicitly set on the table (using setItem()), or for which their data has been set either by the user when editing a cell or programmatically (through setData() of the table model).

selectedItems() works exactly in the same fashion: it only returns existing QTableWidgetItems within the current selection, even though the selection contains other celss.

Try adding the following lines at the end of the __init__:

        self.parmtbl.selectAll()
        print('selectedItems()', len(self.parmtbl.selectedItems()))
        print('selectedIndexes()', len(self.parmtbl.selectedIndexes()))

Even though all enabled cells are selected, the first print() shows absolutely no selected item, although all enabled cells are selected (as the second print() shows).

In your case, when the editing of the cell ends, QTableWidget implicitly creates and set a QTableWidgetItem for that cell, but many (if not all) other cells in the selections are simply "blank", therefore you end up with items only corresponding to cells that have been edited or set.

You can further demonstrate this by manually editing a few cells in the table, then select the whole table and edit a single item: you'll see that only the cells that have been edited are now correctly updated.

The correct solution for this is to rely on the actual selection of the view, which can be retrieved through selectedIndexes(), and contains all QModelIndexes in the current selection model.

In your simple case, you actually don't need to change anything else, as you're accessing functions (row() and column()) that are similar for QModelIndex and QTableWidgetItem:

    def onmulticellchange(self, irow, icol):
        self.parmtbl.blockSignals(True)
        snewval = self.parmtbl.item(irow, icol).text()
        rc = self.oncellchange(irow, icol, snewval)
        print([x.row() for x in self.parmtbl.selectedIndexes()])
        for eachitem in self.parmtbl.selectedIndexes():
            print(self.dfnew["NAME"].iloc[eachitem.row()], rc)
            # etc.

Note that it's common (and preferred) to use a QAbstractTableModel with a QTableView when accessing a pandas model. It looks more complicated than simply using QTableWidget, but in reality is almost always more appropriate, efficient and less prone to implementation bugs.
Do some research on the matter, as there are plenty of resources about this, StackOverflow included.
